title: Words Equal Under Swaps and Relabels
statement:
You may change a lowercase word using two moves, as many times as you like:

  • Swap: exchange the letters at any two positions.
  • Relabel: pick two letters that both already appear in the word and swap them everywhere. For example, relabelling a and c turns "aacb" into "ccab".

Return true if first can be turned into second this way, and false otherwise.

examples.why: Letter counts are a:2 b:3 c:1 and a:1 b:3 c:2. Relabel a and c, then rearrange with swaps.
Relabelling only exchanges letters that are already present, so a d can never appear.
Same letters and same length, but counts {2, 2} cannot become {3, 1}. No move changes how many times some letter appears overall.

constraints: Both words have only lowercase English letters
hints: Swaps let you reorder freely. So only the letter counts matter. What does a relabel do to the counts?
A relabel exchanges the counts of two present letters. It never creates a new letter and never changes the list of count values.
The words are reachable exactly when they use the same set of letters and their sorted lists of counts are equal.

explain.intuition:
Find what the moves cannot change. Swaps only reorder, so the word is really just its letter counts. A relabel exchanges two letters' counts. So the set of letters present never changes, and the multiset of counts never changes; only which letter owns which count does.

Those two invariants are also enough. With matching letter sets and matching sorted counts, relabel letters until each owns the right count, then swap positions into place.
steps: Count letters of both words into two arrays of 26.
For each letter, it must be present in both or absent in both.
Sort both count arrays and compare them element by element.
pitfalls: Checking only the sorted counts. "aab" and "bbc" both have counts {2, 1}, but c is not in the first word.
Checking only the letter set and length, which accepts the third example.
Sorting the words themselves, which compares exact letters and rejects the first example.

solutions.title: Compare letter sets and sorted counts
solutions.idea: The two invariants under both moves are the set of present letters and the multiset of counts.

solutions.title: Count of counts
solutions.idea: Instead of sorting, count how many letters have each frequency and compare those tallies.

followups: Return the minimum number of relabels needed, or −1. How do you match letters to counts?
Relabel may also turn a letter into one that is absent. Which invariant disappears?
lcTitle: Determine if Two Strings Are Close
